I understand this analysis as a heuristic and not rules to follow by the letter.

Disruptive innovation can invalidate the analysis.

For instance, I suspect such type of analysis would have classified web search as a no go domain when Sergey Brin and Larry Page started working on the google web search algorithm. There were plenty search engines provided by the big players at the time.

The added value (or problem solving) criteria is a much better heuristic to determine where to go or not.

column33:
> This fact, while not empirical, is reflected in the literature about humanity.

It seems to me that when you compare what is happening in reality to the 'literature about humanity' they are very different. People are increasingly comfortable with allowing information about them collected and made public online. They are often prepared to give up significant aspects of their privacy for the slightest additional convenience. Check out Google Latitude or Rescuetime for some extreme examples. I fully expect this trend to continue to the point where significant chunks of people's life experience will be stored online.

I'm not sure what humanist literature will have to say about this. If you have an interest in where the world is headed with regards to issues like these you would be better to read some good transhumanist literature instead.

column35: The photographic amateur may be better-educated, better-equipped and better-practiced than the professional. It's not just "anything for a buck", but having a professional attitude toward customer service.
